newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico president urges U.S. renew free trade push.
newsitem.headline: Mexico president urges U.S. renew free trade push.

text.p: President Ernesto Zedillo appealed to the United States on Tuesday to put plans for a free trade zone across the Americas back on track and said Mexico also wanted to bring down barriers to commerce with Europe, the Pacific "tigers" and South America.

In a wide-ranging interview with Reuters, Zedillo also denied reports of a rift between him and his long-ruling party and predicted that Mexico would pull clear of its 1994-95 economic crisis to achieve growth rates of more than six percent a year in the last years of the century.

Noting that progress toward a free trade zone stretching from Alaska to the Antarctic -- pledged by North and South American leaders at a 1994 Miami summit -- had been practically halted this year and much of last because of political opposition in the United States, Zedillo said:
"It is very important that ... there is support from Congress for the Clinton administration so that the momentum in favor of free trade in the Americas can be restarted."
"We need an internal (political) agreement in the United States so that the initiatives of the administration can be translated into real steps of trade opening," he added.

Zedillo, who leaves on Wednesday for a tour of Asia, said Mexico was keen to use the example of its North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) with the United States and Canada to pull down trade barriers with the booming "tigers" of Asia, the European Union and the South American Mercosur trade bloc.
"We believe that if (free trade) is possible, as in Mexico's case, with the United States and Canada, it can be possible between practically any group of countries," he said.
NAFTA, he added, had been such a success that any talk of renegotiating parts of it would be "irresponsible".

Zedillo said Mexico's recent economic growth had lagged behind that of Asian economic stars such as Singapore, South Korea and Taiwan for one fundamental reason: Mexico's lack of home-grown savings to invest in industry and infrastructure.

But he said recent reforms such as the 1997 introduction of private pensions would "give Mexico in a very short time a very similar perspective of economic growth to what we have seen in Southeast Asia, perhaps even better because of (our) natural resources and our geographic location."

The Mexican president strongly denied recent news reports of serious political differences between him and his Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), which has ruled the country continuously for 67 years.

PRI militants openly attacked U.S.-educated government "technocrats" at a party assembly in September, forced the government to limit foreign ownership of the country's petrochemical industry and last week changed various clauses of a key electoral reform law sent by Zedillo to Congress.

Some media speculated that the changes, unusual in a land where the PRI-dominated Congress has traditionally acted as a rubber stamp for the presidential will, signalled a rebellion by party hard-liners against Zedillo's reforms.
Asked about the speculation, Zedillo was categoric. One report, he said, "talks of a rebellion of my party against the president. This is not true".

Zedillo dismissed reported differences between the government's free-market austerity policies and the traditional statist nationalism of party militants as "a problem of communication and of interpretation."
The president also made light of reports that hard-liners from the PRI's old guard -- popularly nicknamed 'dinosaurs' -- were trying to frustrate his political and economic reforms.
"To attribute Mexico's problems to a conspiracy would be a kind of escapism, an escapism from reality," he said.

At the other end of the political spectrum, Zedillo said he hoped to seal a final peace accord with Zapatista Indian rebels in the southern state of Chiapas soon. The Zapatistas, who sent Mexicans and foreign investors into shock with their January 1994 rebellion, "I would not even dare to describe now as a guerrilla group", he added.
